answer:
Okay, so there’s something that I think folks in B2B and SaaS have forgotten over the years.

It turns out if you go back to the early days of salesforce.com, Hubspot, or almost any other company at all today … it was a few people on an email list. It was just a group of passionate customers who were willing to be guinea pigs for some new, untested product and service. And those folks in turn would often help others.

Today we’ve lost that in many cases. We don’t see as much of this anymore. But it’s more important than ever.

A CIO is someone else you can talk about with your customers today, but I just want to share a quick story from the other day at SaaStr Annual 2025. The CEO of a company called Foresight, which did an $8m acquisition by a $1b+ public company. And what’s interesting for us is he started it as his own startup. It was him and two others.

So, that means they went from three to eight or so today. That means 80% of them are still there. But let me tell you, this CIO who bought him in a $8m deal … said the following at SaaStr Annual: “This is the best team I’ve ever worked with.”

The CIO was not just saying that to be nice.

And he also gave some very practical and tactical advice on how to sell to them. He’s got 1,000 engineers under him in this large organization.

So what does it take?

A few things:

First, you have to know who the “CIO” is at a company. It may not always be called that in today’s world of 10-20 different departments and C-level executives for each one. But there are always two or three people you need to talk to.

The first one is what we might call the internal CTO, but more like an IT manager.

They will want to do a free pilot with you before they buy your product.

answer:
So we've had so many great guests on SaaStr this year. But I wanted to do one more deep dive on something that's perhaps less obvious but super valuable. And it is:
How To Truly Stand Out In An Interview
I'm going to share some of the top lessons and tips from our best interviews, from CROs and VPs of Sales all the way up to CEOs.
And you can apply these tips not just when interviewing for a new job — but even if you're looking to get promoted internally. Because in many ways it's much harder than finding your first startup or SaaS job. So let's dive into our top takeaways on what makes an interview truly great, from the CROs and VPs of Sales all the way up to CEOs.
1. Know Everything About The Company, Even Better Than Most Founders
This is probably one of my favorite learnings over the years. If you really know your stuff about a company — especially if it's early stage or growing fast, which in many cases will be true for any SaaS startup today that doesn't have 100+ million in revenue at least — then you can do so much better than most interviewers.
You can learn more here:
How to Research an Unusual Startup
I did this with one of my favorite interviews with the CRO from HubSpot. I asked him a ton about how they sell, and he just got it all right, even some things that were almost wrong in the media. And then when I interviewed the CEO later on, I actually asked him to describe his ideal VP Sales candidate, and what he was looking for — in detail.
He had no idea. He basically only cared about one thing: did they have any experience with HubSpot? That's all that mattered.

So we’re finally back to selling again, with real budgets and new features. And it’s very different than even just 12 months ago.
We’ve all been through this before, but I wanted to summarize why now is a bigger change for sales professionals than any other time in the last decade or so:
#1. The buyers have changed dramatically
There are more of them — and they’re going into buying mode faster than ever. And it’s not just that you’ve got “more” prospects now, or at least, some of them.
It’s actually better for sales people when there is less competition and fewer vendors overall. At least in theory. But the buyers have changed even more dramatically:
They are more distributed
More decentralized
Less centralized buying authority
Even if they aren’t, their expectations to buy faster than ever — with no delays from IT, or marketing, or anyone else
#2. The products have changed as well
So many of us got used to selling the same old product year in and year out for 10+ years.
But now we are all building new “AI” features into our products, that customers don’t really fully understand themselves yet. They know they want AI, but they aren’t sure what it does or how it works — at least not right away.
#3. The sales processes have changed as well
So many of us got used to selling the same old way for 10+ years:
One rep per prospect
A “qualified” lead was just a prospect that said Yes, we’re interested in buying your product now
It’s still true today — but it’s not enough anymore.
Now we have to be more agile. More flexible. And more focused on the buyer themselves than ever before.
#4. The sellers have changed as well
Sales reps are better trained and enabled today than they were 10 years ago, no question.

answer:
So one day, you might wake up and realize it’s been years since your customers actually started growing. Or maybe never really grew at all.
I see this happen often enough, when founders don’t quite understand how the “growth cycle” works in SaaS:
You have to grow fast
to get big.  And then,
you have to maintain a certain growth rate to stay big
.  At least for now, if you’re going more enterprise and bigger deals.
But there’s another phase after that: when your customers are happy enough to keep buying from you year over year without having to recruit new leads all the time.  That can be called “retention” or at least “maintenance”, but it sure is a lot of effort to keep growing in this phase.  And usually, less than in the prior phases.
If you haven’t really achieved NRR (Net Retention Rate) growth by Year 3-4 of SaaS … then something is wrong
.
It could be lack of product-market fit or feature gap for your current customers
. It can take a while to get there, and often it takes an additional phase:
You have to grow fast enough to build the entire team that will support you later.  Then,
you have to maintain a certain growth rate in more enterprise sales (and larger deals) to fuel the team
.
And then when you hit $10m-$20m ARR or so, your customers should be big enough and happy enough with your product to buy from you year-over-year without much recruiting of new leads.  That’s where NRR comes into play as a growth engine — but it will never quite grow faster than the prior phases.
It may take time for your customers to become “happy” enough, or at least big enough and mature enough in their use cases, that they can buy from you year-over-year without recruiting new leads all the time.  And this is often a challenge for founders — because it’s not quite as fun as selling into brand-new logos.
But if your customers aren’t growing with you fast enough to make NRR work as an engine of growth … then something has gone wrong
.  It may have been a feature gap, or product-market fit issue earlier on.  Or even more likely — that sales team hasn’t quite figured out how to sell into the right logos at scale yet.
What happens next is what I call “NRR Death”:
You end up with a company where your only growth engine is recruiting new leads all the time
.  And maybe not even doing it very efficiently or effectively — because you haven’t really gotten NRR working for you as an engine of growth by Year 3-4.
That’s bad enough, but what happens next if you don’t figure out a way to get back on track is that your team can start growing slower than the new leads you are recruiting.

And this isn’t forecasting — it’s reporting. And it might be good enough for reporting … but forecasting? No way. It doesn’t work that well, and a lot of times I think VPs aren’t even really thinking about it deeply at all. They’re too busy closing deals.

So, you're angry. You've had it up to here with our product and our team and how we handle things. I get it.
It's tough when things go wrong at your company. It's worse that the person on the other end of the call is not listening or caring.
I'm going to tell you something that may seem counterintuitive, but trust me: if you don't listen here, and do everything in this post, you'll probably lose the customer anyway. 6 Things You Can Do To Get Angry Customers Back:

#1. Listen to the customer
Don't be defensive. Don't get angry. Just listen. And don't pretend you heard her or him when you didn't, and then tell them what they really meant.
And do it in a way where it's clear that you're listening.

#2. Have The Customer Be Heard by Your Boss (or CEO)
This is usually the #1 thing. If your boss doesn't hear from angry customers, then no one does. And if you don't have someone to listen and fix things, then nothing really gets fixed.
So make sure they are heard.

#3. Send a Real Apology
No one wants an apology that's just a standard form email or call script. We all know those aren't real.
And we will see through them. They don't matter.

But if you send out a real, personal, heartfelt apology from your boss (or CEO) — it may go far in getting things back on track.

#4. Do the Right Thing
This is the most important thing of all
If something went wrong, and they lost data or whatever — fix it

It's not fun to do right now. It won't be easy. But you have to.

#5. Be Honest About What You Will Fix And When (and Why)
Angry customers hate being lied to. They hate broken promises.
But they respect a clear, honest promise of what will get fixed and when

Don't try to hide how long it's going to take or whatever
Just be honest.

This is probably the #1 thing you can do right now
Give them something back for free
It doesn't have to cost a fortune, but if they lost data or whatever — give them some of that back for free

Make sure it's enough and fair.

make sure your boss (or CEO) knows about this.

I guarantee you, in every single situation I've seen over the years where customers were angry … doing these 6 things would have fixed everything.

It’s still true today though — and even more important than ever:
If your AI feature didn’t materially boost revenue, it doesn’t count

Let me give you a few examples:

And so what’s the lesson? Just because you add some “AI” or whatever feature, doesn’t mean it will work. And if it doesn’t materially boost revenue … then it just isn’t important enough right now. You need to try again. Maybe this time with something a bit more proven.

And then when you finally get something working that way…C will fail.
This is the Cowan Paradox in action:
The team’s productivity actually drops because C takes up so much time training and babysitting her, even though she can do some things faster than humans on their own. This pattern has played out in every organization we’ve worked with. The AI agent that was supposed to augment your work becomes a drain – something you have to dedicate more of your team’s attention to.
This is why the “AI Agents Will Let You Do Less Work” narrative doesn’t hold up in practice.

You need custom integrations that no one else does
Your workflows are truly unique and complex — not just different

We use them 24/7, often with critical data

We’ll always have a very deep understanding of the problem and solution — so we can fix it faster than anyone else.
